startup.name: Klaus AI
startup.one_liner: Fast and Safe OpenClaw on the cloud
startup.description: Get your personal OpenClaw instance on the cloud and connected to your Slack or other messaging app in 3 minutes. Pre-installed security features and common skills.

yc_acceptance.basis: Start from about 1 percent with a band of 0.6 to 2 percent (references/yc_acceptance.md). Up: the team of two is technical and the product rides a fast growing open source agent with visible demand. Down: a thin wrapper, copyable by hosting providers and by the project itself, with a single platform dependency (copyable idea with no wedge: defensibility 1 shut down 50 percent). Net about 2 percent.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because a hosted instance of another team's open source agent is a feature that hosting companies and the project maintainers can add, and the security layer is a claim not a moat. Interviewers would ask what the company owns that it cannot lose if the agent's license, maintainers or default settings change.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: seed 49% / 59% / 65%, cond 59% (n=126), months_to_seed 3 / 7 / 15 (n=74). Tag AI cohort: 50% / 61% / 67%. Dev tools tag 2022-2025: seed 50% / 55% / 59%.
anchors.adjustment_reason: The 59% anchor is for ever reaching seed. The forecast window is 10.4 months (from 2026-01-05 to 2026-11-17), and the cohort median time to seed is 7 months with a 75th percentile of 15 months, so about 60 to 70 percent of eventual seeds land inside it. That gives a window anchor near 0.37 to 0.42, and a round must also exceed $1M, which removes YC-deal-only cases. Set at 0.28, about 0.75 times the window anchor, because a hosted wrapper around someone else's open source agent has a thin wedge and a two person team. A named analog, Omnara, shows an agent hosting and control product that did reach a seed, so the discount is not larger.

bands.rationale: Small post YC round of $1M to $3M, usually a pre-seed or angel led round that closes quickly. Cohort data for 2022 and later shows a 25th percentile near $2M, and a team this early often takes the first credible check.
Institutional seed of $3M to $6M, the middle of the 2022 and later table (median $3.2M to $3.5M, 75th percentile about $5M) lifted slightly because only rounds above $1M count here.
Hot sector seed of $6M to $12M. The 2026 winners test found 42 percent of confirmed raises here, but that sample leans to press covered rounds, so this band is held below that share.
Upside band above $12M, reached only with fast revenue or a standout founder story. Rare for a team of this size.

ladder.why_it_fails: Window: 10.4 months, to 2026-11-17. Window: 10.4 months, to 2026-11-17. The product is a managed host for an open source personal agent, and investors will ask what stops the open source project, cloud providers and a dozen hosting startups from offering the same one click install. Revenue per user is likely a monthly hosting fee, which looks like a small business unless the company shows team and enterprise accounts. Omnara and Golf had to broaden into control planes and governance to raise, and a team of two that stays a hosting reseller will likely only close a round under $3M, or none.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: series_a cond 26% (n=74), months_to_series_a 22 / 29 / 38 (n=19). Tag AI: cond 23% (n=66).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Same 10.4 month window as the seed step. The 26% anchor is for ever reaching Series A after a seed, but the cohort 25th percentile for reaching Series A is 22 months from batch start, so only about 10 to 15 percent of eventual Series A rounds close inside a window this short. Set at 0.03 because a hosting wrapper rarely grows into a Series A shaped company inside a year.

bands.rationale: Thin or bridge Series A near the 2022 and later 25th percentile of $11M, taken when growth is real but the story is narrow.
Typical Series A, anchored on the 2022 and later median of $14M to $15M and public medians of $17M.
Upside Series A of $20M or more for a category leader with fast ARR growth, as seen in the top AI cases.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A inside this window would need fast recurring revenue and a defensible product beyond hosting someone else's open source agent. The cohort 25th percentile to Series A is 22 months, and companies that sell managed hosting of open source projects, such as Elementary, took longer and were acquired instead. The more likely situation by November 2026 is a small seed, a pivot, or a stall.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: series_b cond 16% (n=19); calibration sample all years: 44% (n=126).
anchors.adjustment_reason: This step is for ever reaching a Series B given a Series A, with no time window, because recent cohorts are right censored. Set between the recent cohort figure of 16% (n=19, few years of follow up) and the all years figure of 44%, at 0.14 for a conservative read.

bands.rationale: Modest Series B near the 25th percentile of the 2022 and later table ($25M to $27M), likely a flat or small step up.
Typical Series B, median $37M to $40M with post money around $600M in the sparse data.
Upside Series B for a breakout. Few cohort examples, so the band is deliberately small.

ladder.why_it_fails: To reach a Series B the company would need to be the governed enterprise agent platform, not a personal agent host. The underlying open source agent and its large community can ship hosted versions themselves, so the company's growth is capped by a project it does not control, and big cloud platforms can bundle hosting at near zero margin.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only: series_c cond 36% (n=55) across all years. The 2022 to 2025 B2B cohort has no Series C yet (n=3).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Anchor taken from the all years calibration sample because recent cohorts have not had time. Set at 0.25, about 0.7 times the anchor, since most Series B companies in this category face a very crowded late stage market.

bands.rationale: Series C near the 2022 and later 25th percentile ($35M to $50M), in a flat market.
Typical Series C or D, median $74M with post money about $1.2B.
Late stage breakout round. Very few researched cases, so this is a thin tail.

ladder.why_it_fails: Late stage funding would require the company to become a platform with its own agent runtime and enterprise contracts. Mattermost is the example of an open source collaboration company that reached Series B, but it owned the open source project. A company hosting a project owned by someone else has little leverage at that scale.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most paths end in a stall: the underlying agent project changes direction or adds its own hosting, cloud platforms bundle the same thing, and a hosting margin does not fund a team. The company can pivot to governed enterprise deployments, but many analogs that wrapped a hot open source tool shut down or sold small.

killers.risk: The open source agent project or cloud providers ship their own managed hosting
killers.evidence: Hosting vendors such as DigitalOcean and Hostinger already promote managed instances of the same agent and the project itself is growing fast.
killers.mitigation: Own the security, team and enterprise layer, and support several agents rather than one.

killers.risk: Platform dependency on a project the company does not control
killers.evidence: The product name and pitch are tied to one open source agent, and its license, direction or security reputation can change overnight.
killers.mitigation: Abstract over multiple agent runtimes and keep customer data and integrations portable.

killers.risk: Low willingness to pay for a hosted personal agent
killers.evidence: Hosting is priced like a small monthly subscription and individuals can run the same stack on a cheap server.
killers.mitigation: Target teams that need audit, access control and Slack deployments, and sell annual plans.

competition_now.name: DigitalOcean managed agent hosting
competition_now.what: Cloud provider promotes deploying the agent in managed cloud to avoid exposed personal machines.

competition_now.what: Hosting vendor selling managed instances and writing security guides for the same agent.

technical_complexity.rationale: Deploying containers, wiring Slack and shipping preinstalled skills with hardened defaults is a three month job for two engineers. The hard part is genuine security isolation against prompt injection and credential theft, which a small team can only partly solve.

takeover_risk.rationale: Hosting vendors already market managed instances and the project maintainers can add a hosted tier. A rival needs about three months, has distribution and has an incentive because hosting revenue is easy to add.

evidence.claim: Security firms report many exposed self hosted instances of the agent, which creates demand for a safer hosted option.
Hosting vendors write guides arguing managed cloud deployment reduces exposure, showing that the pitch has an audience.

roadmap.goal: Show paying users of the hosted agent and a reason they will not self host.
actions: Launch publicly and publish the number of paid instances
Document a security isolation design and run an outside test
roadmap.proof: At least 50 paying instances and a security review

roadmap.goal: Move from personal hosting to team and enterprise accounts.
actions: Add team admin controls, audit logs and single sign on
Support a second agent runtime to cut single project risk
roadmap.proof: Ten team accounts and $15K monthly recurring revenue

roadmap.goal: Become the governed agent platform, not a host.
actions: Own an orchestration and policy layer customers cannot get from cloud hosting
Sign annual contracts with companies that deploy agents in Slack
roadmap.proof: $1M annual recurring revenue with retention above 90 percent

pros.evidence: Researchers count thousands of exposed self hosted instances, so a safer default has a buyer.

pros.point: Rides fast growing agent demand with a three minute setup
pros.evidence: Slack connected in 3 minutes with preinstalled skills lowers friction for non technical users.

brand.name: Klaus AI
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Klaus AI" --era 2022+: name plus descriptor, 7 characters, 2 syllables, descriptor word ai
weaknesses: A personal name plus the generic suffix AI is hard to own as a trademark and says nothing about security
brand.rationale: A human first name with an AI suffix follows a crowded naming pattern that gives little recall, unlike distinctive invented brands such as Stripe. The effect is neutral because the company's fate will turn on hosting economics and platform risk.

narrative.headline: A fast hosting wrapper around an open source agent with real security demand but very high copy risk.
narrative.general_summary: Klaus AI sells a ready to use, safer hosted instance of a popular open source personal agent, connected to Slack in minutes. Demand exists because self hosted instances have been found exposed, but the hosting layer is easy to copy by cloud providers and by the project itself, and the company depends on one project it does not control. Inside the 10 month window the chance of a round above $1M is below the cohort window anchor, and a Series A is very unlikely. The odds do not rank this company against others.

assumptions: Team of two with no disclosed traction as of 2026-01-05.
Search results dated after the as of date were ignored when judging the market.

The seed probability is for a window of 10.4 months and a round above about $1M. It does not rank this company against others: in the 2026 winners test the average seed probability was 0.65 for companies that raised and 0.62 for companies confirmed to have raised nothing beyond the YC deal.
Series B and C plus steps are for ever reaching the round, not inside the window. Reaching a round years later is common for companies with paying customers.
Knowledge base coverage: calibration cohorts are 2022 to 2025 B2B (n=150 researched), with funding coverage partial for most, so known-only rates are biased low.
